angle: Prediction in Ungauged Basins: what regionalization transfers, and what is the ceiling
verdict: PURSUE THE ATTRIBUTE-CONTENT BRANCH; ABANDON THE DONOR-TRANSFER BRANCH. The classical regionalization families this angle was meant to evaluate (spatial proximity, physical-attribute similarity, attribute regression, donor-catchment transfer) are the wrong tool for this project, and the single verified source says so in two independent ways. First, the only two regionalization rules deployable at an ungauged pin with no local observations are separated by 0.01 R_NP (proximity 0.79 vs attributes 0.78, Pool et al. 2021, 671 catchments, spatial holdout) - so the entire question 'does attribute similarity beat spatial proximity' has a verified answer of 'no, and it does not matter', which retrospectively validates lat/lon already being top-3 features. Second, and decisively, the same paper's own donor-scarcity statistic (at a relative-performance threshold of 0.7, the median hypothetically-ungauged catchment has at most 23 suitable donors out of 670, i.e. ~3.4%) implies an expected suitable-donor count below one at our 19 independent basin families; donor-selection regionalization derives its power from a large diverse pool and that mechanism is structurally unavailable here. Rebuilding the pipeline as a donor-transfer or similarity-weighted scheme is therefore predicted to be a wash at best and is NOT recommended. BUT the angle is still worth pursuing for a different reason than it was posed: Pool et al. hold the attribute set FIXED and vary only the donor-selection rule, so nothing verified here speaks against acquiring BETTER static attributes - and their attribute-only family still delivers +0.09 R_NP over random donors, roughly 70% of the entire realizable no-local-data gain. The actionable output of this angle is consequently not a regionalization method but a data-acquisition target: EPA StreamCat and the USGS Wieczorek NHDPlus attribute series deliver ~2.65-2.7 million CONUS catchments' worth of static basin descriptors ALREADY ACCUMULATED to the upstream watershed of every NHDPlus COMID, which is exactly the object the deployment pipeline already computes via NLDI, and AgTile-US supplies the tile-drainage layer the project has been unable to source. Two hard caveats. (1) EVERY verified number in this angle is streamflow in near-natural CAMELS catchments explicitly screened for minimal human influence - the exact opposite of tile-drained Iowa row-crop basins - and there is ZERO verified water-quality PUB evidence in the corpus, so no published benchmark exists against which LOFO AUC 0.820 / PR-AUC 0.634 can be judged. (2) The corpus contains several tier-3 leads (a nitrate-specific temporal-vs-spatial KGE gap, a donor-count saturation curve, a small-n selection-bias warning) that would materially change the picture if true, and none of them were adversarially verified; they are recorded below as leads with confidence 'unverified' and must not be used as warrant for any decision until checked.

findings.claim: At a target with no local observations, the choice between spatial proximity and physical-attribute similarity as a regionalization rule is a wash: median R_NP 0.79 (distance-only donor selection) vs 0.78 (catchment-attribute donor selection), a gap of 0.01, against a random-donor floor of 0.69-0.70. The fixed-classification family is 0.76. The realizable no-local-data spread over random donor selection is therefore ~0.09-0.10 R_NP. This is the direct verified answer to the angle's core question - attribute-based similarity does NOT beat plain spatial proximity - and it retrospectively validates lat/lon being top-3 permutation-importance features in the current model: proximity is already doing the work an attribute-similarity scheme would do. CORRECTION APPLIED: the frequently-quoted headline 0.82 (distance+volume) is NOT realizable at an ungauged pin; see the separate finding on target-observation requirements. CORRECTION APPLIED: R_NP is the non-parametric variant of the KLING-GUPTA efficiency (Pool et al. 2018), not a Nash-Sutcliffe-type metric; R_KG is the standard KGE and R_NP is the non-parametric analogue OF it, not the reverse. Under R_KG the same three families spread 0.04 rather than 0.02, so the 'wash' conclusion is metric-dependent in magnitude though not in sign.
findings.effectSize: median R_NP: Dist 0.79, Attr 0.78, fixed classification 0.76, Random 0.69-0.70. Deployable-family gap = 0.01 R_NP (0.02 R_KG: 0.64 vs 0.62). Gain of any deployable family over random = ~0.09-0.10 R_NP.
findings.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (leave-one-catchment-out, receiver treated as ungauged) with NO temporal holdout - donors calibrated on 1 Oct 1989-30 Sep 1999 and all approaches evaluated on that same window. No nesting or region blocking, so this protocol is WEAKER than our leave-one-basin-family-out.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The COMPARISON is not reproducible at n=19 - both families select the 3 most similar donors from a pool of 670, and a 3-of-18 selection samples similarity space far too coarsely for the ranking to be meaningful. But the CONCLUSION is safe to act on in the negative direction: if attribute-similarity donor selection cannot beat proximity with 670 donors, there is no basis to expect it to beat proximity with 18. Do not spend engineering effort building a similarity-weighted donor scheme.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: Yes - distance-only and attribute-only donor selection both require zero observations at the target. This is precisely why they are the two families quoted here.

findings.claim: DONOR SCARCITY IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT AND THE PAPER QUANTIFIES IT. With all 671 CAMELS catchments calibrated and each of the other 670 evaluated as a donor: 'For a relative performance value of 0.7, half of the hypothetically ungauged catchments have at most 23 suitable donor catchments' - i.e. only ~3.4% of the candidate pool is usable at that threshold. The paper further reports that for the median catchment MOST donors are worse than random parameter sets ('For the other 60% of the donor catchments, one would be better off using random parameter sets'). DERIVED BY THIS SYNTHESIS (arithmetic, not from the paper): scaling 3.4% to the 18 donor families available to any one of our 19 leads to an EXPECTED suitable-donor count of ~0.6, i.e. under one. Donor-transfer and nearest-analogue regionalization draw essentially all of their power from a large, hydroclimatically diverse pool, and that mechanism does not exist at n=19. This is the strongest verified argument against restructuring the pipeline around donor selection, and it rests on the source's own numbers rather than on assertion.
findings.confidence: verified (the 23/670 and 60% statistics are verified from the primary text; the extrapolation to 0.6 expected donors at n=19 is arithmetic performed by this synthesis and is an order-of-magnitude argument, not a published result)
findings.effectSize: At relative performance 0.7: median catchment has <=23 suitable donors of 670 (3.4%). For 50% of catchments, >60% of donors underperform random parameter sets. Extrapolated to an 18-family pool: <1 expected suitable donor.
findings.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout, exhaustive all-pairs donor evaluation (every catchment treated as hypothetically ungauged against all 670 others)
findings.nBasins: 671 (each evaluated against the other 670 as donors)
findings.feasibilityAtN19: INFEASIBLE, and this is the finding that establishes it. Flagged explicitly per the n=19 rule: the evidence base is ~35x our effective independent-unit count, and the mechanism being measured (selecting a small number of close analogs from a large pool) degrades monotonically as the pool shrinks. Do not propose donor-based regionalization for this project.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: The donor-selection step itself would work at an ungauged pin (distance and attributes are computable there), but the finding is that there will be no suitable donor to select. So: structurally applicable, practically useless at our scale.

findings.claim: POOL ET AL. TESTS DONOR-SELECTION RULES, NOT ATTRIBUTE CONTENT - SO IT IS NOT EVIDENCE AGAINST ACQUIRING BETTER STATIC ATTRIBUTES, AND ARGUABLY ARGUES FOR IT. The study holds a fixed attribute vector (area, aridity, precipitation seasonality, snowfall fraction, wetland fraction, clay fraction, forest fraction) constant across all 19 approaches and varies only how donors are chosen from it. Attribute-based donor selection alone gains +0.09 R_NP over random donors, which is roughly 70% of the entire realizable no-local-data gain (0.09-0.10). The correct reading is therefore: the RULE for exploiting a fixed attribute set is nearly saturated, while the VALUE of the attribute set itself is large and untested at the margin. Critically, that fixed attribute vector contains nothing resembling tile-drainage density, subsurface hydraulic connectivity, or any agricultural-management descriptor - the controls this project independently identifies as dominant in Iowa. This is the finding that redirects the angle from method-selection to data-acquisition, and it is the warrant for the dataset recommendations below.
findings.effectSize: Attribute-based donor selection: 0.78 R_NP vs 0.69 random = +0.09, ~70% of the 0.09-0.10 total realizable no-local-data gain. Marginal value of a BETTER attribute: not measured by this study (fixed attribute set).
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The mechanism this finding points to - concatenating richer static descriptors into a single globally-pooled model - is n-agnostic in a way that donor selection is not. It adds columns to 160,074 rows rather than requiring analogs to be found among 18 peers. It is the one lever in this angle that is NOT obviously blocked by n=19. Caveat: with only 19 independent units, the ability to DETECT a between-site improvement is severely limited; expect wide confidence intervals and pre-commit to repeated/nested CV over families rather than a single LOFO point estimate.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: Yes, and this is the key property. Static basin attributes are map-derivable at any pin from the delineated NLDI basin, with no local observation, no gauge, and no monitored neighbor required.

findings.claim: THE BEST-PERFORMING REGIONALIZATION FAMILIES IN THE LARGEST COMPARATIVE PUB STUDY ARE UNAVAILABLE TO THIS PRODUCT BECAUSE THEY REQUIRE OBSERVATIONS AT THE SUPPOSEDLY UNGAUGED SITE. Pool et al. define Vol verbatim as 'The three catchments with the smallest volume error for the (hypothetically) ungauged catchment are used as donors' - the volume error is computed against the receiver's own measured discharge. The authors state of their category D/E methods that they 'require either estimates of hydrological signatures or a small number of local point observations', and the Plain Language Summary concedes 'volume information is per definition missing in ungauged catchments'. Consequently Vol (0.80), Dist&Vol (0.82), Sign, Dist&Sign, Dist&RMSE and Attr&Sign are partial oracles, Best (0.87) is a full oracle requiring the target's observed hydrograph, and the upper benchmark UB (0.89) is a local calibration scored IN-SAMPLE. Anyone quoting '0.82 is the best regionalization result' in our context is quoting a method that needs field measurements at the map pin. This also means the paper's relative metric R* is measured against an optimistically biased ceiling and must not be read as an out-of-sample skill ratio.
findings.effectSize: Oracle/partial-oracle tier: UB 0.89 (in-sample local calibration), Best 0.87 (needs target hydrograph), Dist&Vol 0.82, Vol 0.80 (need target discharge). Deployable tier: Dist 0.79, Attr 0.78, classification 0.76. The gap between the deployable ceiling (0.79) and the local-calibration benchmark (0.89) is 0.10 R_NP and is the study's own statement of the PUB penalty.
findings.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout for the regionalization approaches; the UB benchmark is in-sample local calibration and is not a holdout number at all
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Not applicable - blocked by the deployment target before sample size becomes relevant. Worth noting for a DIFFERENT product: if a small number of grab samples were ever collected at a candidate pin, this study prices that information at roughly +0.03 R_NP over pure proximity (0.79 -> 0.82). That is a real but modest return, and it is a streamflow-volume result whose transfer to nitrate concentration is entirely unevidenced.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: NO. Explicitly and prominently: the top-ranked regionalization families in this literature all require observations at the target site. The shipped product has none, and only 22 of 85 training sites have discharge at all (zero of the 61 IWQIS sites), so we cannot even build the donor-side signature library statewide.

findings.claim: OUR PROTOCOL IS STRICTER THAN THE PUBLISHED PUB STANDARD, SO OUR NUMBERS ARE CONSERVATIVE RELATIVE TO THE LITERATURE. The standard PUB evaluation - leave-one-catchment-out, each gauged catchment treated in turn as ungauged and predicted from the remaining donors - is what Pool et al. use, and it is spatially held out at the catchment level. But it applies NO nesting or region blocking (donors may be spatially adjacent or hydrologically nested with the receiver) and NO temporal holdout (calibration and evaluation both run 1 Oct 1989-30 Sep 1999). Our leave-one-basin-FAMILY-out design, which groups sites whose basins nest and whose records overlap in time, is materially more conservative. Two consequences: (a) published leave-one-site-out PUB numbers are likely optimistically biased relative to LOFO and are not strictly comparable to our 0.820; (b) the correct reporting discipline, which this paper models well and which we should adopt, is to bracket every result between an explicit LOWER benchmark (random / base-rate, here 0.263) and an explicit UPPER benchmark (a site-calibrated model that has seen the target's own history) and report where in that spread the transfer result falls.
findings.effectSize: Protocol claim, no effect size. The benchmark spread in the source is 0.69 (random) to 0.89 (local calibration), with realizable transfer at 0.79 - i.e. transfer recovers ~50% of the random-to-local-calibration spread.
findings.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout, catchment-level, no temporal holdout, no nesting/region blocking
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Fully feasible and cheap - this is a reporting-discipline change, not a modeling change. Concretely: alongside LOFO AUC 0.820, report (i) the base-rate/random lower benchmark and (ii) an upper benchmark from a model trained WITH each held-out family's own history, then express transfer skill as the fraction of that spread recovered. At n=19 this also makes the wide uncertainty visible rather than hidden.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: Yes - it is a measurement convention, not a method.

findings.claim: THE ENTIRE VERIFIED EVIDENCE BASE FOR THIS ANGLE IS STREAMFLOW IN NEAR-NATURAL CATCHMENTS, AND IS DOUBLY MISMATCHED TO THIS PROJECT. Pool et al. contains no water-quality, nitrate, or concentration content whatsoever: all 671 catchments and all 19 approaches concern daily streamflow, evaluated with KGE-family metrics on hydrographs, and the object being transferred is a calibrated HBV conceptual-model parameter vector - an object with no analogue in a feature-based XGBoost classifier. Separately, the CAMELS gauge set is explicitly screened for 'minimal human influence' (Newman et al. 2015), which excludes precisely the artificially drained, heavily fertilized row-crop basins we model; tile drainage is not represented in HBV at all. Therefore: (a) none of this paper's metrics are commensurable with AUC/PR-AUC on a binary exceedance target, (b) its donor pool contains essentially no hydrologic analog to our target population, and (c) it supplies no method that can be lifted into our pipeline - only a protocol design, a benchmarking discipline, and a ranking of donor-selection heuristics. Its findings transfer to us by ANALOGY only, and that must be stated wherever they are cited.
findings.effectSize: 0 of 671 catchments and 0 of 19 approaches address a concentration or exceedance target. Metric families (R_NP/R_KG on daily hydrographs vs AUC/PR-AUC on binary exceedance) are not intercomparable.
findings.splitProtocol: not-applicable - this is a scope/absence claim
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Not applicable. This finding is a constraint on how every other finding in this angle may be used, not a proposal.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED LEAD - THE NITRATE-SPECIFIC TRANSFER PENALTY. Tier-3 material in this corpus reports that Pandit et al. (2025, WRR, doi:10.1029/2024WR039207) trained an LSTM on high-frequency nitrate sensor data across CONUS and obtained median KGE 0.60 under temporal (within-site 5-fold 80/20) validation versus median KGE 0.18 under spatial validation in unmonitored basins, from the same model - and that restricting the application domain from CONUS to the Mississippi River Basin raised the spatial figure from 0.18 to 0.34. If true, this would be the single most relevant result in the whole angle: a same-paper, same-model measurement of the ungauged-basin penalty for daily nitrate CONCENTRATION, reproducing our 'good timer, mediocre site-ranker' diagnosis at continental scale, plus direct evidence that ATTRIBUTE-SPACE DOMAIN RESTRICTION (not more donors) is what buys ungauged skill - which would make our Iowa-only, agriculturally homogeneous scope an advantage rather than a limitation. THIS IS UNVERIFIED. The extraction states the full text returned HTTP 402/403 on all routes and every number comes from the abstract; the number of sensor sites is unknown (one snippet asserted 95, explicitly flagged as unconfirmed), so the donor-pool regime cannot be established. Do not use any of these numbers as warrant for a decision. Verifying this paper is the highest-value follow-up in this angle.
findings.effectSize: REPORTED BUT UNVERIFIED: median KGE 0.60 temporal vs 0.18 spatial (delta ~0.42, a 3.3x difference from protocol choice alone); 0.18 -> 0.34 under MRB domain restriction (+0.16).
findings.splitProtocol: reported as both - temporal-holdout (5-fold, 80/20 within-site time-series split) and spatial-holdout (entire unmonitored basins) reported separately and explicitly labeled by the authors
findings.nBasins: unknown - abstract does not state the site count; '95 CONUS nitrate sensor sites' appeared in a search snippet and could not be confirmed. Order of magnitude appears to be tens-to-low-hundreds, i.e. the SAME regime as our 85 sites / 19 families, not the CAMELS 531-671 regime - which is exactly why verifying it matters.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Unknown, and that is the point - if the site count really is in the tens, this would be the only PUB evidence in the corpus from a donor regime comparable to ours. Cannot be assessed until the site count is verified.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: Partially. Tier-3 material also indicates the study modeled streamflow and nitrate as two separate LSTMs and that the nitrate pathway may consume discharge; if so, its 0.18 spatial result is an OPTIMISTIC bound for us, since replicating it would require first solving ungauged-basin streamflow for Iowa - a second PUB problem stacked on the first. Also unverified.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED LEAD - TILE DRAINAGE AS THE TOP BETWEEN-SITE DRIVER. Tier-3 material reports that Shapley analysis of the spatially-validated nitrate model in Pandit et al. (2025) identified TILE DRAINAGE density, ROADWAY density and WETLAND COVER as the key spatial drivers of MEAN nitrate concentration - i.e. of the between-site level specifically, not the temporal signal - with non-linear thresholds illustrated by counterfactuals such as reducing tile-drain density from 60% to 0% and doubling wetland cover from 5% to 10%. If true this is continental-scale confirmation that tile drainage is a first-order between-site control and that its absence from our 68-feature set is a plausible primary cause of between_r2 = 0.21. UNVERIFIED: no scalar effect sizes were recoverable, the Shapley magnitudes are in paywalled figures, the site count is unknown, and the tile-drainage layer they used could not be identified from the accessible text. USE AS A LEAD ONLY. Note however that this lead is CONSISTENT with the verified finding that Pool et al. varies donor rules over a fixed attribute set containing no drainage descriptor, and it points at a data gap the project has independently flagged - so it is worth acting on via the dataset recommendation below (AgTile-US), whose value does not depend on this claim being true.
findings.effectSize: REPORTED BUT UNVERIFIED: ranking only - tile drainage, road density, wetland cover as top spatial drivers of mean concentration. No magnitudes recoverable.
findings.splitProtocol: not-applicable (interpretation of a fitted model, though the model interpreted is reported to be the spatially-validated one)
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The implied action - add a tile-drainage basin aggregate as a static feature - is one column on 160,074 rows and is fully feasible. Detecting the resulting between-site improvement at 19 independent families is the hard part; pre-commit to repeated CV and report an interval.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: Yes. Tile-drainage density is a static raster aggregate over the delineated basin, computable at any pin with no local observation.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED LEAD - WATER-QUALITY POOLING BEHAVES DIFFERENTLY FROM STREAMFLOW POOLING. Tier-3 material reports that Gorski et al. (2024, WRR, doi:10.1029/2023WR036591), covering 46 predominantly agricultural midwestern/eastern US sites predicting 7-day mean nitrate concentration, found that 'developing a single model for all sites reduced performance at several locations with distinct characteristics, suggesting that there is a threshold of dissimilarity beyond which more data does not improve the model', and that the authors warn 'While many deep learning studies have shown that national or even global models can outperform local models, it is not clear that this is true for water quality constituents.' The same material reports a four-way pooling comparison (46 single-site models, 5 attribute clusters, 8 glacial-hydrogeologic 'hydro terrane' groups, 1 global model) in which best-model site counts were single-site 16, hydro-terrane 13, global 10, clustered 7 of 46, with the 8 terrane groups achieving median KGE 0.65 and only ONE site with KGE<0 - the fewest catastrophic failures. Read charitably this says attribute-based grouping buys ROBUSTNESS on atypical basins rather than higher median skill. UNVERIFIED throughout - full text returned HTTP 402/403, and the corpus itself flags that the paper appears to contain NO spatially-held-out evaluation at all, meaning every number is temporal holdout at monitored sites and its KGE 0.66 must never be cited as a PUB benchmark. The group sizes (~6-9 sites per group) are the closest analogue in the corpus to our 19 families, which is why this is worth verifying.
findings.effectSize: REPORTED BUT UNVERIFIED: best-model site counts single-site 16 / hydro-terrane 13 / global 10 / clustered 7 (of 46); terrane groups median KGE 0.65, 1 site with KGE<0; single-site median KGE 0.66. Spread across four regionalization families is weak and site-dependent.
findings.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout at monitored sites; the corpus flags that NO spatial/leave-site-out evaluation appears to exist in this paper, but this could not be confirmed against the full text
findings.nBasins: 46 sites (groups of 5 attribute clusters and 8 hydro terranes)
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The grouping idea is the tier-3 family most compatible with n=19 - it requires only that families be clusterable, not that hundreds of donors exist. But note the reported effect is failure-mode reduction on odd basins, not a median lift, and our metric of interest (between_rate_r2) is a median-style quantity. Do not expect this to move between_r2 even if verified.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: Only partially. Assigning a new pin to a group requires attributes at the pin (fine), but every reported skill number presupposes discharge as a required daily input at all 46 sites - which we do not have at the target. Also unverified.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED LEAD - THE DONOR-COUNT SCALING CURVE THE RESEARCH QUESTION ASKED FOR. Tier-3 material reports that Patil & Stieglitz (2012, HESS 16:551-562, doi:10.5194/hess-16-551-2012), over 756 US HCDN catchments under leave-one-out jack-knife with inverse-distance-weighted transfer from the N nearest gauged neighbours, swept N from 1 to 50 and found median Nash-Sutcliffe rising sharply from 0.49 at N=1 to 0.61 at N=4, then only marginally to a maximum 0.615 at N=15, DECLINING beyond 15. If true, the marginal value of donors saturates at ~4-5 and the n=19 constraint would be far less binding for proximity-style donor transfer than assumed. The same material reports two further results that cut the other way: gauge density within 200 km explained only 6% of the spatial variability in skill (R2 = 0.06, robust across 100-500 km radii), and average donor distance explained only 12% (R2 = 0.12, Spearman rho -0.44) - so proximity itself is a real but weak signal. UNVERIFIED, and NOTE THE TENSION WITH VERIFIED EVIDENCE: this curve would soften the verified Pool et al. donor-scarcity finding, but the two are measuring different things (Patil transfers observed area-normalised streamflow from neighbours, which requires gauged donors with concurrent records; Pool measures whether ANY donor's calibrated parameters transfer acceptably). Where they conflict, the verified claim wins: at n=19 the expected number of SUITABLE donors is under one, and a saturation curve over unsuitable donors is not reassuring. Verify before relying on it.
findings.effectSize: REPORTED BUT UNVERIFIED: median NS 0.49 (N=1) -> 0.61 (N=4) -> 0.615 max (N=15) -> declining. Gain 1->4 donors = +0.12 NS; gain 4->15 = +0.005 NS. Separately R2=0.06 for gauge density, R2=0.12 for donor distance.
findings.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (leave-one-catchment-out jack-knife; predictions built only from other catchments' observed streamflow)
findings.nBasins: 756 (CONUS HCDN, drainage area 23-5000 km2, median 715 km2, WY1970-1988)
findings.feasibilityAtN19: This is the only candidate curve in the corpus bearing directly on the n=19 question, which makes verifying it the second-highest-value follow-up after Pandit et al. If it holds, it argues n=19 is not fatal for proximity-style transfer specifically; it does NOT rehabilitate attribute-regression or global attribute->level learning, which is our actual architecture.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: NO for the method measured. IDW transfer of area-normalised observed streamflow requires GAUGED donors with concurrent records - and for nitrate we would need concurrent nitrate records at donors, which exist only at our 85 sensor sites. The curve is informative about donor economics; the method itself is not deployable at an arbitrary pin as a nitrate predictor.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED LEAD - THE CLASSICAL RANKING AND THE FAILURE OF ATTRIBUTE REGRESSION. Tier-3 material reports that Oudin et al. (2008, WRR 44(3), doi:10.1029/2007WR006240), over 913 French catchments with two lumped rainfall-runoff models, found the ranking spatial proximity > physical similarity > regression-on-attributes, with the abstract stating verbatim that 'The regression approach is the least satisfactory, with results very close to those obtained using one median parameter set for the whole country' - i.e. at n=913 donors, regressing model behaviour on catchment physical attributes recovered essentially NO between-catchment information beyond a single global constant. The companion Oudin et al. (2010, doi:10.1029/2009WR008887, 903 catchments) reportedly found that the pool of physically-similar catchments overlaps significantly with the pool of behaviourally-similar catchments for only 60% of catchments, and diagnosed the cause as SUBSURFACE: 'the role of the underground properties of the catchment on its hydrological behavior was not found to be accurately described by the available physical descriptors'. UNVERIFIED - both papers are paywalled (HTTP 403), no per-method NSE values were recoverable, and one extraction explicitly flags that its mapping of six NSE values to (method, model) pairs was INFERRED from a secondary meta-analysis's method-code ordering and should not be trusted. The ordinal ranking is corroborated in direction by the VERIFIED Pool et al. result (Dist 0.79 > Attr 0.78), so the direction is safe; the magnitudes are not. The subsurface diagnosis, if verified, would be independent literature support for prioritising a tile-drainage / subsurface-connectivity covariate over further weather feature engineering - which is the direction this angle's verdict already recommends on verified grounds.
findings.effectSize: REPORTED BUT UNVERIFIED: ordinal ranking only (proximity > similarity > regression ~= single national median parameter set); all three 'lag far behind' full local calibration. Oudin 2010: physical-similarity and behavioural-similarity pools overlap significantly for only 60% of catchments (40% failure rate). Numeric NSE values NOT recoverable and one corpus extraction's NSE mapping is self-flagged as inferred.
findings.splitProtocol: reported as spatial-holdout (each catchment treated in turn as ungauged, donors from the remainder), but one extraction states the protocol 'could NOT be determined from accessible metadata' - treat the protocol label itself as unconfirmed
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The negative result, if verified, is a caution rather than a method: attribute REGRESSION on catchment descriptors failed to beat a global constant at n=913, 48x our independent-unit count. That is a warning against expecting a static-attribute regression to learn absolute level. Note it does NOT indict attribute CONCATENATION inside a pooled nonlinear model, which is a different estimator from the linear-regression-on-attributes family these papers tested.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: Yes for the families described - proximity, physical similarity and attribute regression are all computable with no target observations. That is why the negative result matters.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED LEAD, AND IT CONFLICTS WITH THE VERIFIED EVIDENCE - ATTRIBUTES BEATING LAT/LON. Tier-3 material reports that Willard et al. (2024), training on 782 CONUS stream-temperature sites and testing on 580 DIFFERENT spatially held-out sites, found that adding latitude/longitude/elevation to a meteorology-only LSTM produced almost no gain at unmonitored sites (median RMSE 1.77 -> 1.72 degC, delta 0.05) whereas adding GAGES-II static catchment attributes to that same location-aware model gained 0.25 degC (1.72 -> 1.47) - a ~5x larger effect, with the authors stating location information 'did not meaningfully improve performance'. The same material reports that a single pooled CONUS LSTM beat every regionalized alternative at unmonitored sites (median per-site RMSE 1.43 vs 1.98 for per-HUC-2-region models, 2.02 for attribute-cluster models, 2.00 for multi-task), winning in 14/17 regions and 14/15 clusters. CONFLICT NOTED AND ADJUDICATED: the VERIFIED Pool et al. result has distance-based donor selection slightly AHEAD of attribute-based (0.79 vs 0.78). These are not strictly contradictory - Pool measures a donor-SELECTION rule while Willard measures INPUT FEATURES inside one pooled model, and the two are different mechanisms - but they push in opposite directions on the angle's central question, and per the tier rules the verified claim wins where they genuinely conflict. The honest synthesis is: as a donor-selection metric, attributes and proximity are equivalent (verified); as model INPUTS, attributes may carry substantially more than lat/lon (unverified). Our architecture is the latter case, which makes verifying Willard et al. valuable. UNVERIFIED throughout; also stream temperature only, with no nitrate or nutrient content whatsoever.
findings.effectSize: REPORTED BUT UNVERIFIED: meteo 1.77 -> +lat/lon/elev 1.72 (delta 0.05) -> +GAGES-II attributes 1.47 (delta 0.25) degC median per-site RMSE. Pooled 1.43 vs regional 1.98 / cluster 2.02 / multi-task 2.00; pooled wins 14/17 regions, 14/15 clusters. Also reported: observed streamflow as an input (1.57) helped LESS than static attributes (1.47).
findings.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (single train/test site split, 782 train / 580 held-out, no site in both) - a genuine ungauged-basin protocol, though single-split rather than k-fold
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Flagged per the n=19 rule: all conclusions rest on 780-1,350 donor sites, and the corpus explicitly notes no ablation reduces donor count below ~780, so this paper gives ZERO evidence about behaviour at 19 independent families. Its own data-volume comparison reportedly showed that ~1.6x more sites produced only 'similar or modest' improvement while feature richness dominated - which if verified would be a useful argument that ATTRIBUTE COVERAGE beats DONOR COUNT, the most n=19-friendly finding in the corpus.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: Yes for the winning configuration - meteorology plus static basin attributes, no discharge and no local history required. The corpus reports the authors' headline conclusion is that streamflow is NOT necessary for accurate prediction at unmonitored sites, which if verified would directly address our 22-of-85 discharge coverage problem by saying the coverage sacrifice is not worth making.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED LEAD - SMALL-n STUDIES ARE THE HIGHEST-VARIANCE, MOST SELECTION-BIASED STRATUM OF THE PUB LITERATURE. Tier-3 material reports that Parajka et al. (2013, HESS 17:1783, meta-analysis of 34 studies / 75 results / 3,874 catchments) found that 'the 21 studies with less than 20 catchments have the largest scatter in the performance because of the smallest sample size', that 'as the number of catchments increases the performance tends to decrease', and that the authors attribute the small-n advantage to selection bias rather than method quality: 'in some of the studies with few catchments, these catchments were hand picked in terms of suitability for regionalisation'. Also reported: 'The maximum performance exceeds 0.8 for the similarity, regression and model averaging methods, but this performance is documented only for the small datasets' and 'the performance of similarity-based regionalisation is clearly lower for assessments with large datasets.' If verified this is a direct methodological warning for us: at 19 families we sit in the stratum whose reported NSE spans roughly 0.3-0.9, meaning any single-number regionalization gain we measure carries scatter comparable to that entire range, and an improvement smaller than roughly 0.05 in our transfer metrics is not distinguishable from donor-set luck. UNVERIFIED - not adversarially checked. This is an argument for repeated/nested CV over families and reported confidence intervals, NOT for abandoning the work.
findings.effectSize: REPORTED BUT UNVERIFIED: strata <20 / 20-200 / >200 catchments; median NSE band roughly 0.5-0.75 across strata with the <20 stratum spanning ~0.3-0.9. Result counts by method: 33 spatial proximity, 9 similarity, 12 model averaging, 17 parameter regression, 4 regional calibration.
findings.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout throughout (Level 2 by leave-one-out with each gauged catchment treated as ungauged; Level 1 aggregates study-reported ungauged-mode results)
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Directly about n=19 and therefore worth verifying, but note the implication is a statistical-power caution rather than a method. Actionable regardless of verification status: any between-site improvement we report should come with an interval computed over repeated family partitions, because a point estimate on 19 units is not decision-grade.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: Not applicable - methodological finding about the literature.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED LEAD - COMMONLY MIS-CITED PUB EVIDENCE, AND A CHEAP DIAGNOSTIC WE CAN RUN. Tier-3 material reports that Kratzert et al. (2019, HESS 23:5089-5110) did NOT test prediction in ungauged basins - the paper reportedly states 'we never ask our model to predict in a basin where it did not see training data', training on 1999-2008 and evaluating on 1989-1999 for the SAME 531 CAMELS basins - so every NSE in that widely-cited paper is a TEMPORAL holdout on gauged basins and is not comparable to any leave-one-basin-out number. If correct, this matters because that paper is routinely cited as PUB evidence (its actual PUB companion is reportedly Kratzert et al. 2019 WRR, doi:10.1029/2019WR026065, using k-fold spatial holdout). The same source material reports two further items worth noting as leads: that removing the 27 static CAMELS attributes and training on meteorology alone reportedly collapsed mean NSE by ~0.44 (the extraction explicitly flags the no-static row as second-hand and needing verification against Table 3), and that the entity-aware architecture bought essentially nothing over a plain LSTM fed the same statics (+0.01 mean NSE, within noise). ACTIONABLE REGARDLESS OF VERIFICATION: the reported attribute-corruption test - adding Gaussian noise to standardized static attributes and observing median NSE degrade smoothly from 0.71 at sigma=0 to 0.48 at sigma=1.0 - is a cheap ablation we can replicate at n=19 as a diagnostic. If our skill is genuinely attribute-driven rather than lat/lon identity-memorization, jittering the statics should degrade skill smoothly and monotonically; a cliff would indicate the model is memorizing site identity via coordinates. That test is worth running on our own model independent of whether the published numbers verify.
findings.effectSize: REPORTED BUT UNVERIFIED: EA-LSTM vs LSTM+statics +0.01 mean NSE (within noise); ~+0.44 mean NSE from adding 27 static attributes (no-static row self-flagged as needing verification); attribute-noise degradation median NSE 0.71 -> 0.48 across sigma 0 -> 1.0.
findings.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout - and the whole point of the lead is that this paper is frequently mislabeled as spatial. Its numbers must NOT be compared to our LOFO 0.820 under any circumstances.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The noise-injection diagnostic is trivially feasible at n=19 - it is an ablation on our existing model, costs one training sweep per noise level, and directly tests whether lat/lon dominance reflects real geographic signal or site memorization. Recommended regardless of the paper's verification status. The 531-basin performance numbers themselves are flagged as far outside our regime and are not usable.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: The diagnostic is an offline model audit, not a deployed method - so yes, applicable, but it produces information rather than skill.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED LEAD - GAUGE-DENSITY THRESHOLDS PUT IOWA AT OR BELOW THE POINT WHERE PROXIMITY-BASED TRANSFER DEGRADES. Two tier-3 items converge on this. First, Lebecherel, Andreassian & Perrin (2016, J. Hydrol. 539:196) reportedly degraded the French network under a 'hydrometrical desert' protocol (progressively deleting the CLOSEST gauges to the target) and found spatial-proximity performance deteriorates strongly below roughly 0.6 gauges per 1000 km2 - the extraction explicitly flags that this threshold came from a SECONDARY SUMMARY, not the paywalled primary text, and is unverified. Second, Parajka et al. (2013) reportedly quote Oudin et al. (2008) as finding that proximity's advantage over similarity vanishes once gauge density falls below ~60 gauges per 100,000 km2. DERIVED ARITHMETIC (by this synthesis, over Iowa's ~145,746 km2): 85 sensor sites = 0.58 per 1000 km2 and 58 per 100,000 km2 - AT both thresholds; 19 independent basin families = 0.13 per 1000 km2 and 13 per 100,000 km2 - roughly 4.5x BELOW. If either threshold verifies, the prediction is that (a) further squeezing the spatial-proximity family has little headroom for us, and (b) swapping our lat/lon proximity signal for an attribute-similarity donor scheme should be a wash, not a win. Note (b) is independently supported by the VERIFIED 0.79-vs-0.78 result, so the conclusion does not depend on these unverified thresholds - they only supply a mechanism for it.
findings.effectSize: REPORTED BUT UNVERIFIED: proximity performance deteriorates below ~0.6 gauges/1000 km2 (threshold from a secondary summary); proximity-vs-similarity advantage vanishes below ~60 gauges/100,000 km2. Iowa equivalents derived by this synthesis: 0.58 per 1000 km2 / 58 per 100,000 km2 at 85 sites; 0.13 / 13 at 19 families.
findings.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout with deliberate network degradation (Lebecherel); spatial-holdout leave-one-out under progressively thinned donor networks (Oudin via Parajka)
findings.nBasins: French national dataset, same family as the 913-catchment Oudin set; exact retained counts not verified
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The arithmetic is the finding: at 19 families we are far below both quoted thresholds. This reinforces the verified donor-scarcity conclusion from a second direction. It also implies the site-count-to-area ratio, not the row count, is the relevant scale parameter - a useful framing when arguing that 160,074 site-days does not mean 160,074 units of between-site information.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: Not applicable - a property of the donor network, not a method.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED LEAD - CROSS-REGION TRANSFER LEARNING HAS A DOCUMENTED FAILURE MODE WHERE THE SMALL LOCAL DATASET WINS. Tier-3 material from a 2025 survey (arXiv:2308.09766) reports that 'Le et al. (2022) transfer ML streamflow models built on North America to data-poor South Africa and Central Asian regions and find that the LOCAL models trained on MINIMAL DATA OUTPERFORM the models from data-rich regions', and separately that in a hybrid-modeling context 'the output from the NWM actually impairs the model and prevents it from learning generalizable hydrological relationships'. This is the most directly relevant published caution against the obvious n=19 remedy of pre-training on a large external corpus (CAMELS, or a national nitrate dataset) and fine-tuning on Iowa. It does NOT say local always wins; it says the direction is not guaranteed and must be measured. UNVERIFIED, with no magnitudes, no site counts, and an unspecified internal split. ACTIONABLE FORM: any transfer-learning or external-pretraining proposal for this project must ship with an Iowa-only baseline run under the identical LOFO protocol, and must be abandoned if it does not beat it.
findings.effectSize: REPORTED BUT UNVERIFIED: direction only - local minimal-data models outperformed transferred data-rich-region models; magnitude not given in the survey.
findings.splitProtocol: unknown - cross-region transfer means the target geography is unseen by construction, but the internal split is not specified in the survey text
findings.nBasins: unknown - North America source pool, South Africa / Central Asia targets; counts not given
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Highly relevant precisely because n=19 makes external pretraining tempting. The finding is a required guardrail on that idea rather than an argument against trying it.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: Yes in principle - a pretrained-then-finetuned model needs no target observations. The caution is about whether it helps, not whether it deploys.

datasets.name: EPA StreamCat - Accumulated Landscape Attributes for NHDPlusV2 (v2.1) Catchments, Conterminous US
datasets.url: https://www.epa.gov/national-aquatic-resource-surveys/streamcat-dataset (API and R package: https://github.com/USEPA/StreamCatTools ; bulk FTP: https://gaftp.epa.gov/epadatacommons/ORD/NHDPlusLandscapeAttributes/StreamCat/)
datasets.resolution: NHDPlusV2 catchment (COMID) - ~2.65 million stream segments and their catchments across CONUS. Every metric is served in TWO forms: Cat (local catchment only) and Ws (full accumulated upstream watershed).
datasets.years: Varies by metric layer; includes contemporary and multi-date land-cover, PRISM climate normals, agricultural nitrogen inputs, soils, geology, and hydrologic-modification metrics. Most are static or few-epoch, not daily.
datasets.access: Free. Three routes: (1) REST API, (2) the StreamCatTools R package which wraps the API and is also reachable from nhdplusTools via source='streamcat', (3) bulk download by region/state/county from the EPA gaftp server. No authentication.
datasets.license: US Federal government work / EPA public data - public domain, no restriction. Cite the StreamCat data release.
datasets.coversMultiState: YES - full conterminous US. This is the property that matters most here: the project's current inner-join against Iowa-only crop and N-surplus grids silently under-counts for the largest multi-state basins, and StreamCat's Ws accumulation is computed over the true CONUS network, so basins extending into Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, South Dakota or Illinois are handled correctly by construction.
datasets.whyUseful: This is the single highest-leverage acquisition implied by the verified findings. The verified evidence says the donor-selection RULE is saturated but the attribute SET was never varied - and StreamCat is the largest ready-made static attribute set in existence for exactly the spatial object this pipeline already computes. The deployment target delineates an upstream basin via USGS NLDI, which returns COMIDs; the project already stores an NHDPlus comid per basin. So the entire feature-construction step reduces to a keyed lookup rather than on-the-fly raster aggregation - no new geoprocessing, no Iowa-boundary clipping, and no per-pin latency cost beyond an API call.
datasets.howToIncorporate: At training time, for each of the 85 sensor basins take the stored outlet COMID and pull the Ws (watershed-accumulated) variants of a targeted subset: PctCrop2019Ws / PctHay / PctUrbMd (land cover), Fert / Manure / CBNF agricultural-nitrogen-input metrics, ClayWs / SandWs / OmWs / PermWs / RckDepWs (soils), BFIWs (base-flow index), ElevWs and its derivatives, WetIndexWs (topographic wetness), and PctImp. Each arrives as a single basin-level scalar already accumulated upstream, so each becomes ONE new static column appended alongside the existing lat, lon, log_basin_area, mean_dist_to_sensor, max_dist_to_sensor block - no distance-bucket expansion, which is deliberate: the existing distance-bucket machinery is what produced the failed temporal ablations, and the verified diagnosis points at basin-integrated static level, not spatial structure. At inference time, resolve the map pin to a COMID via NLDI and issue the identical StreamCat API lookup. Evaluate under the existing LOFO protocol and report between_rate_r2 with an interval over repeated family partitions, since at 19 units a point estimate is not decision-grade. IMPORTANT ORDERING NOTE: add these as a single block and ablate the block, not variable-by-variable - with 19 independent units, per-variable selection will overfit the fold structure.
datasets.limitations: Most StreamCat layers are static or coarse-epoch, so they contribute only to the between-site term - which is exactly the term we are targeting, but it means zero expected gain on within_r2. The agricultural-nitrogen-input layers overlap conceptually with the existing gTREND N-surplus features and carry the same broadcast-forward-in-time hazard that already failed here (-0.166); use them as static basin descriptors only, do NOT construct a time-varying series from them. Metric vintages differ across layers, so a basin's attribute vector mixes epochs. Finally, adding many columns at n=19 independent units risks fitting the fold structure - the block-ablation discipline above is not optional.

datasets.name: USGS Select Attributes for NHDPlus Version 2.1 Reach Catchments and Modified Network Routed Upstream Watersheds for the Conterminous US (Wieczorek, Jackson & Schwarz; ver. 5.0, June 2025)
datasets.url: https://www.sciencebase.gov/catalog/item/5669a79ee4b08895842a1d47 (parent series; component releases include Select Basin Characteristics https://www.sciencebase.gov/catalog/item/57976a0ce4b021cadec97890 , Select Geologic Attributes https://www.sciencebase.gov/catalog/item/5703c816e4b0328dcb82295a , Base Flow Index https://www.sciencebase.gov/catalog/item/5669a8e3e4b08895842a1d4f )
datasets.resolution: NHDPlusV2.1 reach catchment (COMID), ~2.7 million stream segments; provided both as local catchment values and accumulated upstream through the river network.
datasets.years: Layer-dependent. Includes 30-year climate normals (e.g. 1971-2000 rainfall/runoff R-factor), NWALT anthropogenic land-use trends, modeled historical land use and land cover 1940-1990, and static geology/soils. The historical LULC series is the notable time-varying component.
datasets.access: Free bulk download of tabular CSV/ZIP from USGS ScienceBase. No authentication, no API key. Programmatic access via the ScienceBase item REST endpoints.
datasets.license: USGS public-domain data release. Cite the specific component data release DOI.
datasets.coversMultiState: YES - conterminous US, network-routed accumulation, so multi-state basins are correct by construction.
datasets.whyUseful: Complements StreamCat rather than duplicating it. Two components are specifically valuable here: (1) the geologic/lithologic attributes, which speak directly to the unverified-but-plausible Oudin et al. (2010) diagnosis that the missing regionalization information is SUBSURFACE rather than surface land use; and (2) the modeled historical LULC 1940-1990 series, which offers a legacy-land-use descriptor - relevant because our N-surplus product ends in 2017 and the legacy-nitrogen pathway is the mechanism most often invoked for between-site level differences in agricultural basins. Same COMID key as StreamCat, so both attach to the existing pipeline through one join.
datasets.howToIncorporate: Join on the same outlet COMID already stored per basin. Pull the accumulated-upstream variants of the geologic attributes (e.g. dominant lithology fractions, carbonate/sandstone/unconsolidated fractions) and Base Flow Index; each becomes one static basin-level column. For the historical LULC component, do NOT build a time series - instead derive one or two static summaries such as 'fraction of basin in cropland in 1950' and 'change in cropland fraction 1950-1990' as legacy-land-use descriptors, again one static column each. Append to the same static block as the StreamCat variables and ablate the combined block under LOFO.
datasets.limitations: Overlaps StreamCat substantially for soils and land cover - pull only the non-redundant geologic and historical-LULC components to avoid inflating the column count at n=19. Version 5.0 (June 2025) supersedes earlier versions and column definitions have changed across versions, so pin the version. The historical LULC layers are MODELED reconstructions, not observations, and their uncertainty is not propagated. Bulk-file only for some components, so ingestion is a batch job rather than a per-pin API call - for inference, pre-materialize a COMID-keyed lookup table rather than fetching at request time.

datasets.name: AgTile-US - 30 m Tile-Drained Cropland Map of the Conterminous US (Valayamkunnath et al. 2020)
datasets.url: https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/AgTile-US/11825742 (paper: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x ; also mirrored as a Google Earth Engine community dataset at https://gee-community-catalog.org/projects/tile/ )
datasets.resolution: 30 m raster, binary (0 = undrained agricultural land, 1 = tile-drained agricultural land).
datasets.years: Single epoch, built from the USDA 2017 Census of Agriculture county-level tile-drainage statistics, NLCD 2016 cropland, SSURGO soil-drainage class, and SRTM slope. No time series.
datasets.access: Free public download from figshare in GeoTIFF and NetCDF. No authentication, no request needed. Also directly usable in Google Earth Engine via the community catalog, which avoids downloading a CONUS-scale 30 m raster.
datasets.license: Scientific Data / figshare open data release - CC BY 4.0 expected; confirm on the figshare record before redistribution. Cite Valayamkunnath, P., Barlage, M., Chen, F. et al. Sci Data 7, 257 (2020).
datasets.coversMultiState: YES - full conterminous US at 30 m, so the multi-state portions of the largest basins are covered at the same resolution as the Iowa portions. This directly addresses the known inner-join under-count problem, which the project notes is worst for the largest multi-state basins.
datasets.whyUseful: This closes the project's most conspicuous data gap: tile drainage is flagged internally as the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa, absent from the 68-feature set, with NO data source identified. AgTile-US is that source. It is also the concrete instantiation of the verified finding that Pool et al. varied donor rules over a FIXED attribute set containing no drainage descriptor - i.e. the untested margin. Independently, the (unverified) Pandit et al. Shapley result names tile drainage as the top spatial driver of MEAN nitrate concentration, which is the between-site level term specifically. The recommendation does not depend on that unverified claim: the verified argument is that attribute content is the unexhausted lever and this is the highest-prior missing attribute.
datasets.howToIncorporate: Create ONE primary feature, tile_drained_fraction_basin = (count of AgTile-US cells with value 1 within the delineated upstream basin) / (count of cells classified as agricultural land within that basin), computed over the whole basin as a single scalar - deliberately NOT split into the existing 3 distance buckets on the first pass, since the verified diagnosis is a basin-integrated level deficit rather than a spatial-structure deficit and the distance-bucket expansion triples the column count against 19 independent units. Optionally add a second scalar tile_drained_area_km2 (drained cells x 900 m2) to separate intensity from extent. Validation accuracy is reported at 82.7-93.6% over the heavily tile-drained Midwest, which is the relevant subregion, so treat the fraction as reliable for Iowa. If and only if the basin-integrated version shows a between_rate_r2 gain under LOFO, THEN test the 0-2 km riparian-bucket variant, since the riparian bucket previously helped CLF (+0.039 PR-AUC) while hurting REG. Evaluate under LOFO with an interval over repeated family partitions.
datasets.limitations: BINARY, not a drainage-intensity or drain-spacing measure - it answers 'is this cell drained' rather than 'how intensely', so it may not resolve between-site differences among uniformly-drained Iowa basins, which is precisely our hardest discrimination problem. This is the main risk to the recommendation and should be stated when reporting the result. Single epoch (2016/2017 inputs), so no temporal variation - contributes only to the between-site term. It is a MODELED product downscaled from county-level census totals using soil drainage class and slope, so within-county spatial pattern is inferred rather than observed, and errors will be spatially correlated at the county scale - which, given that our CV folds are basin families, could correlate with fold structure. CONUS 30 m is a large raster; prefer the Earth Engine route or pre-compute a basin-keyed lookup rather than rasterizing per request at inference time.

refuted.claim: That Pool et al. (2021)'s headline 'best regionalization' result of median R_NP 0.82 (distance + volume) represents an achievable ceiling for a regionalization scheme at an ungauged site.
refuted.correction: REFUTED by the paper's own method definitions. Vol is defined as selecting 'the three catchments with the smallest volume error for the (hypothetically) ungauged catchment' - computed against the receiver's measured discharge - and the authors state category D/E approaches 'require either estimates of hydrological signatures or a small number of local point observations', with the Plain Language Summary conceding 'volume information is per definition missing in ungauged catchments'. At a target with genuinely no local observations the best method in the study is Dist at 0.79, so the realizable spread over random donors is ~0.09-0.10 R_NP, not 0.13. Any citation of 0.82 in this project's context is a citation of a method requiring field measurements at the map pin.

refuted.claim: That R_NP is a Nash-Sutcliffe-type efficiency and R_KG is its Kling-Gupta analogue.
refuted.correction: REFUTED and inverted. R_KG is the standard Kling-Gupta efficiency (Gupta et al. 2009); R_NP is its NON-PARAMETRIC variant (Pool, Vis & Seibert 2018), using Spearman rank correlation and a normalized flow-duration-curve error. Neither is a Nash-Sutcliffe-type efficiency, and the derivation runs from R_KG to R_NP, not the reverse. Separately, the paper's RELATIVE efficiency is a distinct metric R*_NP (percent improvement over random donors, bounded by local calibration) and must not be conflated with R_NP.

refuted.claim: That the Pool et al. benchmarks (upper benchmark 0.89, best-donor 0.87) represent achievable out-of-sample performance.
refuted.correction: REFUTED. Both are oracles. UB is a local calibration scored IN-SAMPLE on the target's own observations (calibration and evaluation both run 1 Oct 1989-30 Sep 1999, with only 2 preceding years as warm-up). Best requires knowing the target's observed hydrograph in order to rank donors by R_NP. Consequently the relative metric R* is measured against an optimistically biased ceiling and must not be read as an out-of-sample skill ratio. The achievable no-local-data range is 0.76-0.79 against a 0.69-0.70 random floor.

refuted.claim: That Pool et al. (2021) shows improving static between-site descriptors (e.g. acquiring tile-drainage data) is futile because attribute-based selection scored only 0.78.
refuted.correction: REFUTED as a misreading. Pool et al. hold the attribute set FIXED (area, aridity, precipitation seasonality, snowfall fraction, wetland fraction, clay fraction, forest fraction) and vary only the donor-SELECTION RULE. The study therefore says nothing about the value of a BETTER attribute, only about the value of a better rule for using a fixed one. Moreover attribute-based selection alone gains +0.09 R_NP over random - roughly 70% of the entire realizable no-local-data gain - so if anything the result argues that attribute information is load-bearing. The fixed vector notably contains no tile-drainage or subsurface-connectivity descriptor.

refuted.claim: That the three 'single-information' families (volume 0.80, distance 0.79, attributes 0.78) constitute an equal-cost menu from which one may freely choose, making the choice 'nearly a wash'.
refuted.correction: PARTIALLY REFUTED. The scores are a wash but the DATA REQUIREMENTS are not: volume/signature methods require the target's own observations while distance and attributes do not. For this project the menu is only Dist 0.79, Attr 0.78, classification 0.76 versus random 0.69, so the deployable spread is 0.01 rather than 0.02. Note the underlying conclusion gets STRONGER for us, not weaker. A second caveat: 'nearly a wash' is a MEDIAN-only statement that the paper explicitly warns against - approaches 'differ considerably in their poorest performance values leading to clear differences in the suitability of the approaches' (under random donors 44 of 671 catchments fell to R_NP between -0.2 and -11.6), and under R_KG the same three families spread 0.04 rather than 0.02. Per-catchment, the best method varies widely (Dist&Vol best for 22%, Dist&Sign 12%, Vol/Sign 9%).

refuted.claim: That Pool et al. (2021) tested 19 regionalization approaches, without qualification.
refuted.correction: MINOR CORRECTION - the source is internally inconsistent, not the claim. The abstract and Section 2.3.1 say 19 regionalization approaches and 'a total of 23 methods', but the Table 2 caption reads 'Description of the 18 Regionalization and 4 Benchmark Approaches Tested in This Study' (=22). Following the abstract and main text is the defensible reading; cite as '19 approaches (Table 2 caption says 18) plus 4 benchmarks'. Separately, the effective n is BELOW 671 for the Climate class, WB class and Sign class approaches: 'Ungauged catchments that did not belong to any class were excluded from the evaluation.' The 671 figure is exact for the dataset and for flexible-donor approaches, not uniformly for all methods.

refuted.claim: That Pool et al. (2021)'s protocol is directly comparable to this project's leave-one-basin-family-out CV.
refuted.correction: REFUTED as stated. The Pool protocol is spatially held out at the catchment level - genuinely so, the receiver's own data are never used to predict it - but it applies NO nesting or region blocking (donors may be spatially adjacent to the receiver) and NO temporal holdout (calibration and evaluation both run 1 Oct 1989-30 Sep 1999). It is therefore WEAKER than LOFO, and our numbers are likely conservative relative to published leave-one-site-out PUB results. Additionally the metrics are not commensurable at all: R_NP/R_KG on daily hydrographs versus AUC/PR-AUC on a binary exceedance target.

refuted.claim: That Kratzert et al. (2019, HESS 23:5089-5110) provides prediction-in-ungauged-basins evidence.
refuted.correction: REPORTED AS REFUTED BY TIER-3 MATERIAL, ITSELF UNVERIFIED. The extraction states the paper says 'we never ask our model to predict in a basin where it did not see training data', with training on 1999-2008 and evaluation on 1989-1999 for the SAME 531 CAMELS basins - making every NSE a temporal holdout on gauged basins, not a PUB number, and not comparable to LOFO 0.820. The actual PUB companion is reportedly Kratzert et al. 2019 WRR (doi:10.1029/2019WR026065) with k-fold spatial holdout. This correction was NOT adversarially verified and is recorded here because the mis-citation is common enough to be worth flagging; verify before relying on it.

uncovered: NO VERIFIED WATER-QUALITY PUB EVIDENCE EXISTS IN THIS CORPUS. The angle explicitly asked for 2-3 papers doing water-quality PUB rather than streamflow PUB. Zero such papers survived verification. Both tier-1 claims are Pool et al. (2021), which is entirely streamflow and contains no nitrate, concentration or exceedance content. Every water-quality candidate in the corpus (Pandit et al. 2025 nitrate LSTM; Gorski et al. 2024 nitrate at 46 sites) is tier-3 and was reachable only through paywalled abstracts (HTTP 402/403 on all routes tried, including Wiley landing pages, pdfdirect, DOAJ, USGS Pubs Warehouse, with no preprint located). CONSEQUENCE, stated plainly: there is NO published water-quality-PUB benchmark against which LOFO AUC 0.820 / PR-AUC 0.634 can be compared, and every verified effect size in this angle transfers to nitrate by ANALOGY ONLY. Any recommendation asserting that a regionalization technique 'works for water quality' on the strength of this literature is unsupported.

THE SKILL-VERSUS-NUMBER-OF-DONOR-CATCHMENTS CURVE WAS NOT OBTAINED IN VERIFIED FORM. This was the angle's most decision-relevant request. The only verified quantity bearing on it is Pool et al.'s donor-scarcity statistic (median catchment has <=23 suitable donors of 670 at a 0.7 threshold), which is a scarcity RATE at fixed pool size, not a curve over pool size - Pool et al. never vary the donor pool, which is fixed at 670 for every catchment. The one actual curve in the corpus (Patil & Stieglitz 2012: median NS 0.49 at N=1 -> 0.61 at N=4 -> 0.615 at N=15, declining beyond) is tier-3 and unverified, and measures donors USED per prediction rather than pool SIZE available - a related but distinct quantity. VERIFYING PATIL & STIEGLITZ IS THE HIGHEST-VALUE REMAINING ACTION FOR THIS ANGLE after Pandit et al.

NO VERIFIED EVIDENCE AT ALL EXISTS BELOW ~650 DONOR CATCHMENTS. The verified evidence base is a single study at n=671. Every tier-3 lead sits at 46, 148, 531, 671, 756, 782-1362, 903 or 913 catchments. Nothing verified, and almost nothing unverified, speaks to the n=19-independent-families regime. The one tier-3 item that addresses small-n directly (Parajka et al. 2013: studies with <20 catchments show the largest performance scatter, attributed to hand-picking selection bias) is unverified and is a warning about variance, not a skill estimate. We therefore CANNOT state what between-site skill is attainable at n=19; we can only state that the donor-selection mechanism which produces published gains is absent at that scale.

NO VERIFIED BETWEEN-BASIN R2 OF SITE MEANS - THE EXACT QUANTITY THE RESEARCH QUESTION ASKED FOR - WAS FOUND IN ANY SOURCE. The question asked what between-basin skill (R2 of site means or equivalent) published studies attain with fewer than ~100 donor catchments. No source in the corpus, verified or unverified, reports a between-site R2 of site means. Published PUB studies report median per-site efficiency (NSE, KGE, R_NP), which mixes the within-site and between-site terms and cannot be decomposed post hoc from published summaries. Our within_r2 0.42 / between_r2 0.21 decomposition has NO published counterpart to be compared against. This is a genuine gap in the literature's reporting conventions, not merely a gap in this search.

THE VERDICT ON ATTRIBUTE SIMILARITY VERSUS SPATIAL PROXIMITY SPECIFICALLY IN FLAT, AGRICULTURALLY HOMOGENEOUS REGIONS IS NOT ESTABLISHED. The verified answer (0.79 vs 0.78, a wash) comes from 671 CAMELS catchments explicitly screened for MINIMAL HUMAN INFLUENCE - the exact opposite of the tile-drained, fertilized, artificially drained Iowa row-crop population, which is systematically screened OUT of CAMELS. The donor pool therefore contains essentially no hydrologic analog to our target basins, and no verified source stratifies the proximity-versus-attributes comparison by terrain or by agricultural intensity. A tier-3 item reports flat humid catchments landing predominantly in a middling predictability group, but that is unverified and concerns streamflow.

HIERARCHICAL / PARTIAL-POOLING REGIONALIZATION - one of the five families the research question named - PRODUCED NO VERIFIED EVIDENCE WHATSOEVER. Pool et al. does not test it. The nearest tier-3 analogues are Gorski et al.'s attribute-clustered and hydro-terrane group models (unverified, temporal holdout only, n=46) and the survey's claim that entity-aware attribute concatenation supersedes the functional-similarity premise (unverified, qualitative, no head-to-head effect size). A properly hierarchical / partial-pooling formulation with a site-level random effect shrunk toward an attribute-predicted mean - which is arguably the most statistically natural response to 19 independent units and 160k rows - is UNADDRESSED by any source in this corpus, verified or otherwise. It is neither supported nor refuted here, and the absence should not be read as a negative result.

THE TILE-DRAINAGE LAYER USED BY THE ONE CONTINENTAL-SCALE NITRATE PUB STUDY COULD NOT BE IDENTIFIED. Tier-3 material reports Pandit et al. (2025) used a CONUS-wide gridded tile-drainage product in the Shapley analysis that ranked tile drainage as the top spatial driver of mean nitrate, but the paywalled text did not expose the source. AgTile-US is recommended above as an independently-verified substitute that meets the operational criteria, but it is NOT confirmed to be the same product, and if the study used a drainage-INTENSITY rather than binary layer that difference would matter, since binary coverage may not discriminate among uniformly-drained Iowa basins.

NO SOURCE, VERIFIED OR UNVERIFIED, ESTABLISHES A CONSENSUS BENCHMARK OR ACCEPTABILITY THRESHOLD FOR UNGAUGED-SITE SKILL. There is no published answer to 'what AUC or PR-AUC at an unmonitored site is good enough to ship'. The Pool et al. benchmarking discipline (bracket the result between an explicit random lower benchmark and a locally-calibrated upper benchmark, then report the fraction of that spread recovered) is the closest thing to a standard and is the recommended substitute, but it is a reporting convention rather than a threshold.
